canonicalExplanation.summary: To change a page, first **find** the element: `document.querySelector(".greeting")` returns the first match or **null** if nothing matches, so check before using it. Then **update** the smallest thing that changed: `textContent` for plain text, `classList.add/remove/toggle` for styling state, `setAttribute` or a property like `input.value` or `button.disabled` for behaviour. `textContent` never parses HTML, so user text shows up as text. `innerHTML` parses markup and must never receive untrusted input.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body: A welcome banner shows `Hello, ${name}!` using innerHTML. One learner signs up with the name `` and the page runs their script for everyone who sees it. querySelector is null-checked before textContent updates trusted text without parsing HTML. In this lesson you'll implement a DOM update without unsafe HTML parsing or unnecessary tree replacement. ```predict {"question": "`el.textContent = \"Asha\"` shows…", "options": ["Asha in bold", "the literal characters Asha"], "answer": 1, "why": "textContent sets plain text. The angle brackets are displayed, not parsed."} ```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Scope, closures and modules** module, the **Semantic multi-page site** you built, **Document tree and DOM concept** (the page as a tree of nodes), and **Dependency boundaries**, because DOM code belongs in the view layer.

sections.heading: The rule: find, check, change the smallest thing
sections.body:
```js
function showGreeting(name) {
  const el = document.querySelector("#greeting");
  if (!el) return;                       // missing element: nothing to update.
  el.textContent = `Hello, ${name}!`;    // text only, never parsed.
}

const saveBtn = document.querySelector("#save");
saveBtn?.classList.add("is-busy");       // styling state.
if (saveBtn) saveBtn.disabled = true;    // behaviour via property.
saveBtn?.setAttribute("aria-busy", "true");
```

| Goal | Use |
|---|---|
| show user or plain text. | `textContent`. |
| toggle a visual state. | `classList.toggle("open")`. |
| form value or disabled. | property: `input.value`, `btn.disabled`. |
| ARIA or data attribute. | `setAttribute("aria-expanded", "true")`. |
| insert markup you wrote. | build nodes (next lesson), not innerHTML with data. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why not replace the whole section's innerHTML on each update?", "answer": "It destroys and rebuilds every node, dropping focus, input values and event listeners, and it risks injecting untrusted HTML."}
```

examples.title: Showing a learner's name safely
examples.situation: querySelector is null-checked before textContent updates trusted text without parsing HTML.
walkthrough: **Bug:** `` banner.innerHTML = `Hello, ${name}!` `` runs markup hidden in the name.
**Null-check:** `const el = document.querySelector("#greeting"); if (!el) return;` avoids a crash on pages without the banner.
**Update:** `` el.textContent = `Hello, ${name}!` `` renders the name as text; a test will check the text contains "<img" literally.
examples.result: Every learner's name displays exactly as typed, and no name can run code on the page.

examples.title: The tabs that stayed active
examples.situation: A tab switcher calls `document.querySelectorAll(".tab").classList.remove("active")` and the console shows "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'remove')".
walkthrough: querySelectorAll returns a NodeList, not one element.
A NodeList has no classList, so the call fails.
Fix: loop with for...of and update each tab's classList, then add active to the clicked one.
examples.result: Only the clicked tab is marked active and the others lose the class.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: innerHTML and textContent are interchangeable for displaying user text.
misconceptions.correction: innerHTML parses its string as HTML, so user text can inject elements and scripts. textContent sets plain text and is the safe choice for any text that isn't markup you wrote yourself.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "Showing a learner's name safely", what did innerHTML do with the name?

analogy.example: textContent is like **writing on a sticky note**: whatever you write is just words. innerHTML is like **handing someone building instructions**: if a stranger wrote the instructions, they can make the builder do anything.
usefulFor: null-check = checking the note's spot exists
limitations: Notes can't hold images; textContent really is text only.
Instructions you wrote yourself are fine; that's what building nodes is for.

remediation.explanation: Before each update ask: **Could this element be missing? → null-check. Is this text? → textContent. Is it state? → classList or a property.** If you typed innerHTML with a variable, stop.

recap.summary: To implement a DOM update without unsafe HTML parsing, query the element, null-check it, and change the smallest thing: textContent for text, classList for state, properties or setAttribute for behaviour. Loop over querySelectorAll results, and avoid rebuilding trees with innerHTML.
